episodes.request: We are about to cut release candidates for 2.9.0. What does `vercmp bump pre` do to a version that is already a release candidate, and what does --preid change? Please explain it from the code; no changes.

steps.thought: The README describes the bump command; start there.
steps.output:
# vercmp

Compare, sort, and bump semantic versions. The release scripts use vercmp to find the
newest release tag of a service, to list tags in release order for the release
dashboard, and to work out the next version number. How versions are written and
ordered is described in [docs/VERSIONING.md](docs/VERSIONING.md), which release
engineering maintains.

## Usage

    node --experimental-strip-types bin/vercmp.ts compare 2.7.1 2.10.0
    node --experimental-strip-types bin/vercmp.ts sort tags.txt
    node --experimental-strip-types bin/vercmp.ts sort --reverse tags.txt
    node --experimental-strip-types bin/vercmp.ts latest tags.txt
    node --experimental-strip-types bin/vercmp.ts latest --pre tags.txt
    node --experimental-strip-types bin/vercmp.ts bump minor v2.7.1
    npm run vercmp -- sort tags.txt

- `compare A B` prints `-1`, `0`, or `1` when A is lower than, equal to, or higher
  than B.
- `sort FILE` prints the versions of FILE from lowest to highest, each as it is
  written in the file; `--reverse` prints the highest first. Versions that are equal
  (they differ only in build metadata) keep the order of the file.
- `latest FILE` prints the highest version of FILE that is not a prerelease; `--pre`
  includes prereleases. When there is none, it prints a message and exits with
  status 1.
- `bump LEVEL VERSION` prints the next version. LEVEL is `major`, `minor`, or
  `patch` (that number goes up, the numbers after it go back to 0, and any
  prerelease part is dropped), `pre` (the next release candidate: `2.7.1` gives
  `2.7.2-rc.1` and `2.8.0-rc.1` gives `2.8.0-rc.2`; `--preid beta` uses another
  name), or `release` (drops the prerelease part). A leading `v` is kept.

A version file has one version per line, such as the output of `git tag --list`.
Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are skipped. A version may start with `v`.
A version that cannot be read stops the command with a message that names its line,
and the command exits with status 2. So do a file that cannot be read and a command
line that vercmp does not understand (it prints the usage).

## Library

    import { compareVersions, latestVersion, sortVersions } from "./src/index.ts";

    compareVersions("2.7.1", "2.10.0");        // -1
    sortVersions(["v2.10.0", "v2.7.1"]);        // ["v2.7.1", "v2.10.0"]
    latestVersion(["2.8.0-rc.1", "2.7.1"]);     // "2.7.1"

`parseVersion` and `formatVersion` read and write single versions, `bumpVersion`
computes the next version, and `readVersionList` reads a version file. Functions that
read versions throw a `VersionError` for a text that is not a version.

## Development

    npm test

There are no dependencies: the code is TypeScript run directly by Node 22 with
`--experimental-strip-types`, and the tests use `node:test`. Changes are listed in
[CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md).

steps.thought: The bump rules themselves are in src/bump.ts.
Check how the command line hands --preid to bumpVersion.

finish.thought: nextPrerelease in src/bump.ts covers the three cases, and the command line only passes the name through.
finish.report: `vercmp bump pre` calls bumpVersion in src/bump.ts with the level pre, and nextPrerelease picks one of three cases. If the first prerelease identifier is the prerelease name (rc unless --preid says otherwise) and the second one is a number, the number goes up by one and anything after it and any build metadata are dropped: 2.8.0-rc.2 becomes 2.8.0-rc.3. Any other prerelease of the same release starts the name at 1 without changing MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: 2.8.0-beta.4 becomes 2.8.0-rc.1, and so does a bare 2.8.0-rc. A release starts the first candidate of the next patch: 2.7.1 becomes 2.7.2-rc.1. --preid only changes the name: src/cli.ts reads it with parseArguments and passes it to bumpVersion, falling back to DEFAULT_PREID (rc). A name that does not start with a letter is rejected with a VersionError, which the command reports with exit status 2. A leading v on the version is kept.

episodes.request: The nightly release job stopped with `vercmp: line 14: not a version: "v2.9.0-rc.01" (leading zero in 01)`. What makes a version unreadable, and where does that message come from?

steps.thought: Parsing a single version happens in src/version.ts.
The line number comes from reading the version file; that is src/list.ts.
See where the error is caught and turned into the message and the exit status.

finish.thought: The message is built in three layers: parseVersion, readVersionList, and main.
finish.report: parseVersion in src/version.ts trims the text and matches it against MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with an optional leading v, an optional -prerelease part, and an optional +build part. When the pattern does not match it throws a VersionError `not a version: "<text>"`; when it matches, it still rejects a leading zero in MAJOR, MINOR, or PATCH or in a prerelease identifier made only of digits, an empty identifier, and a number too large to be exact, with the reason in parentheses. Build metadata may have leading zeros. readVersionList in src/list.ts reads the file line by line, skips blank lines and lines starting with #, and puts `line N: ` in front of the message, counting every line from 1. main in src/cli.ts catches the VersionError, prints `vercmp: ` and the message on stderr, and exits with status 2. So line 14 of the tags file has v2.9.0-rc.01: the 01 identifier has a leading zero, and v2.9.0-rc.1 is the readable form.
